topic: Proof of Snell's Law via Fermat's Principle
target_audience: First-year university physics students or advanced high school students

sections.title: The Hook: The Lifeguard's Dilemma
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'Least Time' using a relatable analogy. Light doesn't just travel in a way that minimizes distance, but in a way that minimizes time. This sets the conceptual stage for Fermat's Principle without jumping straight into equations.
sections.example: An animation of a lifeguard (Character) on a beach needing to reach a swimmer in the water. The lifeguard runs faster on sand than they swim in water. To reach the swimmer fastest, they shouldn't run in a straight line; they should stay on the sand longer to maximize speed before entering the water.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Index of Refraction
sections.content: Define the relationship between the speed of light in a vacuum (c), the speed in a medium (v), and the refractive index (n). Visualizing light as a wave slowing down and its wavelength shortening helps ground the math.
sections.example: A split-screen graphic showing light moving through air (n=1) vs. water (n=1.33), with a 'speedometer' icon showing v = c/n.

sections.title: Geometric Setup of the Boundary
sections.content: Establish a coordinate system. Place Point A in Medium 1 and Point B in Medium 2. Define the interface as the x-axis. Identify the variables: horizontal distance (d), heights (a and b), and the transition point (x).
sections.example: A clear 2D diagram where a light ray travels from A(0, a) to a point P(x, 0) on the interface, then to B(d, -b). Use bright, contrasting colors for the two media.

sections.title: The Time Equation Construction
sections.content: Using the Pythagorean theorem, express the total travel time (T) as the sum of time spent in Medium 1 and Medium 2. T = (Distance1 / v1) + (Distance2 / v2).
sections.example: The formula T(x) = [sqrt(x² + a²) / v1] + [sqrt((d-x)² + b²) / v2] appears on screen, with the corresponding triangle segments pulsing to show where each term comes from.

sections.title: Calculus: Minimizing the Path
sections.content: Apply Fermat's Principle by finding the derivative of Time (T) with respect to the position (x) and setting it to zero (dT/dx = 0). This identifies the point of 'Least Time'.
sections.example: A step-by-step calculus animation showing the power rule and chain rule application. The derivative results in: [x / (v1 * sqrt(x² + a²))] - [(d-x) / (v2 * sqrt((d-x)² + b²))] = 0.

sections.title: The Geometric Substitution
sections.content: Link the algebraic derivative back to the physical angles of incidence (θ1) and refraction (θ2). Show that x/L1 is sin(θ1) and (d-x)/L2 is sin(θ2).
sections.example: Superimpose 'sin(θ1)' and 'sin(θ2)' over the corresponding ratios in the equation. The equation simplifies to: sin(θ1) / v1 = sin(θ2) / v2.

sections.title: The Final Reveal: Snell's Law
sections.content: Replace the velocities (v) with (c/n). The 'c' terms cancel out, leaving the final, elegant form of Snell's Law.
sections.example: The final transition: (n1 * sin(θ1)) / c = (n2 * sin(θ2)) / c, leading to the glowing conclusion: n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2). Use an Archer fish (Animal) aiming at a bug as a real-world application of this math in nature.
